utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. A few small matters. First of all, Mr. O'Sullivan, translation was done orally from what the Chamber understands, just for your information since you asked for it. Then the Chamber received follow-up information on what exactly happened with flak jacket and handcuffs. Information is available to the parties. We'll keep you updated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Plavsic, I do understand that no handcuffs, no flak jackets are applied any more and we received information on what happened exactly earlier. Then, Ms. Plavsic, we'll continued today and questions will be put to you by the Prosecution and the Defence. I'd like to invite you to focus your answers very much on what exactly was asked. If we need more further contextual information the parties will certainly ask you for it. But please first focus on the questions themselves which would certainly help us to get through this as quickly as possible, which I understand you also -- is also your wish. Then needless to say that it's the responsibility, professional responsibility of the parties to keep this focus and do whatever they're professionally expected to do in order to achieve that. Finally, Mrs. Plavsic, I'd like to remind you as I always do at the beginning of a day that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Finally, the parties are, when I'm informed that the time reserved yesterday that if the time allocated to the parties at this moment if they would keep some time in reserve for later questions that they will decide themselves how much time, of course, within certain limits to reserve and we try, I said we try to finish today if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just ask for guidance on that because we seek guidance and clarification. The e-mail we received yesterday evening, we confess, was a bit -- slightly puzzling to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not seen an e-mail of yesterday evening. I didn't follow the e-mail exchange of messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's in -- very short, Your Honour. It's so short Your Honour won't have any difficulty. It was an e-mail from one of Your Honour's legal officers and the key point was "the time allotted to each one of the parties as explained in court today," no problem up to that point, "includes any time for further cross." Do we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are supposed that I said yesterday one hour and 20 minutes for the Prosecution, two hours and 40 minutes for the Defence. What we intended to say is that -- of course, you never know what kind of questions will come up, but if you want to reserve some time for questions and response to what the other party has asked that the party itself is responsible for reserving that time. So that means that the -- it means that if you would consider advise to reserve 20 minutes then you should take one hour to start with and then of course there's 20 minutes left at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's helpful guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, Mr. Harmon, who is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, interpreters note we would like to introduce a correction to yesterday's transcript at page 43, line 19. Instead of Karadzic full stop it should say Karadzic and Krajisnik full stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A correction was made to the transcript of yesterday. The parties received it. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me begin by what -- offering what may be reassurance to you but just by way of an indication to the Court and the parties that I expect to be very brief this morning and will only be asking you a relatively few questions so if there's any degree of stress associated with the anticipation of a lengthy questioning from the Prosecution, I wanted to put your mind to rest at the outset. I'd like to begin, however, with a slight procedural matter that I raise the with the Court and with the parties earlier and that's with respect to appears to be a translation error in the transcript of the excerpted portions from Mrs. Plavsic's book. Mr. Stewart and Mr. Josse, I believe, are already aware of that. It appears at page 10 of the translated excerpts, which reflects an excerpt from the book beginning at page 201. And it is the long paragraph that begins with the words Cutileiro's plan. It's about 15 lines from the end of that paragraph and it's the sentence that: "And the institutions in charge of obtaining this information which were responsible for this, i.e., responsible people in these institutions, thought they could only release this information to the president of the municipality," is the current translation. That's end quote. Looking at the B/C/S, I believe that the English translation should properly read at the end of the sentence "president of the Assembly." And it was suggested to me when I raised that with the court officer and with the Defence that the most efficient way of addressing it would be in the manner I'm doing so now, by bringing it to the attention the Court. The Court could then ask the interpreters for the appropriate clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 201. I did not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, it should read "The president of the Assembly" in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We receive confirmation now that it should be "The president of the Assembly." Yes. That's confirmed which the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, I see you looking in the book. Just by way of explanation, it was only a question of how the language that appears in your book was translated and there just seems to be a slip. It's now been corrected. I wanted to ask you, Mrs. Plavsic, about a term you used in connection with the body that was discussed during the course of your interview and then appeared in your statement, and that is the body that was referred to in the statement I believe at paragraphs 36 through 40 as the Supreme Defence Council. In connection with that, I went back to the transcript of the interview you had with Mr. Nielsen and looked in particular at tape 8, page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know. The witness doesn't -- does the witness have the full transcript of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. It's in English in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You read it to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have it. Mr. Tieger will read the literal text as it has been transcribed from the audio, so please listen carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Court and the parties, the portion I'm referring to is at tape 8, page 9, or if you have it sequentially numbered as I do, it would be page -- I believe beginning at page 171.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it might be better, Mrs. Plavsic, if I paraphrase this first and see if you recall it because the thrust of it is not the precise language but the exchange that took place more generally. At that point you were first asked about meetings other than the Presidency and Assembly that you attended with Mr. Krajisnik, and you indicated that there was an abbreviation for something, and I think you said it existed in peace and war in one state, and you were struggling for the name of that body initially, and then it continued --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you seemed to recall at the bottom of that page that there was -- it brought to mind a body that existed in Montenegro, and you referred to Milo Dzukanovic in Montenegro. At that point you still it hadn't recalled the particular name of the body you were trying to think of in response to Mr. Nielsen's question, and then about five pages later during the course of the discussion when -- when you started talking about this further, Mr. Nielsen started to say, "this body that we don't," I presume you were saying we don't have a name for, and then it seemed that the term Supreme Defence Council at that point popped into your head. Now, it does appear to be the case that in fact there is a supreme -- body called the Supreme Defence Council in the SFRY and has existed for some time, but we have not seen any records for a body known as the supreme Defence council, a body by that precise name in the RS in 1992 through 1995, and I wanted you to take a look at this next document which can be distributed. It's the minutes of the meeting of the Supreme Command of the army of Republika Srpska held on 20 December, 1992. And while that's being distributed I wanted to ask you one more question, and that was it appeared also that you were indicated in the interview and I believe in the statement as well, although I'd have to double-check, that this particular body dealt in particular with the issue of supplies and logistics for the army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to explain one thing. If you analyse the name Supreme Defence Council, and we also had another council and you did encounter the name of that council here and that is the political council of the SDS, we talked about terminology on the first day. It's quite different when you have an institution that is named council. The council counsels, but it's not binding. That's how it was in the political council of the SDS. The political council of the SDS in relation to a certain situation would say, "We would advise that such-and-such a thing be done," but this was not binding on the SDS. In the same way the Supreme Defence Council --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I appreciate that and it may be the question I have for you is a little bit simpler than that rather than delving into the precise functions of either body you mentioned just now. My question is simply in light of the fact that you seem to be struggling a bit for the precise name of the body when you first discussed it, I simply -- and then remembered it as something to a body that existed in Serbia and Montenegro or in SFRY by that name. I wanted to ask you if in fact the body you were referring to was known as the Supreme Command rather than the Supreme Defence Council and that's why I wanted to take a look at these -- at these particular minutes, which --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That was the supreme Defence council. And now that you were reading some parts of the transcript, I remember the moment when I told Mr. Nilsson really. I can't remember, but I told him probably I will remember it during the interview, and the whole process of my recollection actually is evident from the transcript. There is a clear difference between bodies that make decisions such as the Supreme Command and the Supreme Defence Council. The Supreme Defence Council provides advice or counsels, and I remember the topics discussed at the Supreme Defence Council. Are we going to have money to by saurkraut because that is the only source of vitamin C for the soldiers during winter. Do we have shoes and so on. Let's say it would be a logistics topic and General Djukic, who was in charge of that, he was the one who would bring up the army requirements at the Supreme Defence Council. It wasn't a body that -- I don't know -- that was in command of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you remember when the body known as the Supreme Command was establish?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as the Supreme Command is concerned, there was a Supreme Commander. When that body was organised, I don't know. I think that when I fled to Pale it was already set up. There was a government. The Assembly was there from much earlier. The Presidency as of the 12th of May, the army on the May of 12th at that meeting in Banja Luka, but I wasn't there. There as nothing strange about that, I think, but I'm not sure whether that exists in other countries as well. But it was, as you know, and I know -- I see that you know that there was such a body in the SFRY and now reading in the papers I see the Supreme Defence Council of Serbia, the Supreme Defence Council of Montenegro. This is the information that I have. In the literal sense of the word council, it's the one who gives counsel. So a body that provides counsel is not a binding body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one minute. And just last question about that subject. Apart from the existence the Supreme Commander, do you recall a body known as the Supreme Command in RS in 1992 through 1995?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At any point in 1992 and then -- or at any point thereafter.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a Supreme Defence Council. The president of the republic was the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Plavsic. Now, one more subject I wanted to address, and that's in reference to something in your statement and in your interview. It appeared and I'm looking at paragraph 30 of your interview and then I'll be looking at a portion of -- excuse me, paragraph 30 of your statement and I'll be looking at a portion of the interview. You indicated your belief that some of the minutes of the Presidency may have been written after, sometime after the meeting took place and the events took place. Again, if I look back to the actual interview that you had with Nilsson and that on tape 4 at page 15, I think that would be -- again, I don't know if the parties have a sequential version. It would be page 86 of the sequential version. You seem to indicate there would be a couple of reasons why you felt that would be the case. One was -- one was your recollection that a number of the minutes indicate -- were signed by -- were signed by Dr. Karadzic as president rather than president of the Presidency, and he wasn't president until December 1992 or January 1993, as you said. And secondly, that you saw some -- or you recalled some minutes that referred to the -- to Republika Srpska rather than a Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you recall that exchange during the course of your interview?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I remember very well because these papers, not just the minutes but I also received from the Prosecution before my sentence was passed I had the opportunity to see some decisions signed by President Karadzic, and I remembered at the time what technical means we had to write. At the time, I recall that we had two Olympia typewriters. I -- I -- there was no computer, at least not in the beginning. So this was something that interested me, so I looked into it. All the minutes were usually not longer than one page. Also, they would begin by saying the meeting began at 8.00 or 9.00, something like that. I'm telling you this because of the sleeping patterns of Mr. Karadzic, his habit of sleeping late. So it rarely started at that time. I'm almost sure that it never started at that time. It even says what time the meeting finished, implying that we had somebody who took the minutes. But it's evident this was written by a person, probably the secretary in his office who had a certain idea of how minutes should look. But when I asked the question why were the minutes not being taken, I was told, well, Mr. Karadzic just dictates the conclusions of the meetings to his secretary later. That's how it was. For such a serious situation, and even if it hadn't been that serious, as far as I was concerned this for me was a strange, very casual approach to that. As for the signatures, I found six or seven only in the material I received. When there was no Republika Srpska, it was called differently, it would state Republika Srpska when Mr. Karadzic was still not President of Republika Srpska but was the president of the Presidency. Sometimes in the papers it would say the President of Republika Srpska, and it was my impression, and I think I wrote that in my book as well, that it was my impression that some of the material, the documents, I don't know how to say it differently, but to say that it was manufactured or fabricated and sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me address very quickly, if I may, a number of the factors you just mentioned. First of all, the minutes of the Presidency are available and have been available to the Court and to the parties for quite a long time. I took the opportunity to look through those minutes. I'm not going to go through those with you one by one. That would be a lengthy and I think quite unnecessary process, but the -- with respect to the usage of Republika Srpska versus Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, looking at those minutes they seem to reflect the following, and again either the Defence or the Court can and no doubt will look at this, that throughout the course of the minutes from the beginning in May until -- throughout 1992 they refer continuously to or the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The first reference to Republika Srpska, that is the Presidency of Republika Srpska, I found was in October, and I think you'll agree it was in -- that the matter was first raised in the Assembly, that is the change of the name of the state was first raised in the Assembly in August, and the formal change took place at the session of the Assembly on September 14th through 15th. So thereafter, the appropriate title of the state would indeed be Republika Srpska; correct? And the minutes would --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a problem when I was writing my book. I didn't know exactly. I couldn't remember exactly when the name was changed. When I talk about that, I'm not just talking only about the minutes. I also had the opportunity to look at some orders from 1992. I received that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... moment. So let me move to the next issue, the next aspect of what you said regarding the minutes. With regard to the usage of the term "President" versus "President of the Presidency," again I look through those and they seem to consistently, at least in the minutes, irrespective of what you might have seen in any orders, reflect the term "President of the Presidency" throughout the course of the minutes. Now, I'd also like to mention to you at least a couple of examples that indicate that those minutes were taken and existed contemporaneously, and I have documents available for you to look at, if necessary. Please tell me if you want to see those, but perhaps it would expedite matters if I indicated to you what those documents contain, first, and then if that's sufficient we can proceed. So in the Presidency minutes of June 10th, they reflect that the Presidency reached a number of conclusions and tasked the government to prepare proposals concerning them, and then although -- I don't know if you saw or looked at the minutes of the government sessions that took place, but then in the government session that took place a few days later on June 15th -- I'm sorry. I know Mrs. Plavsic said something. I didn't hear a translation.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to see minutes of cabinet sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we have those in evidence, and the Court and the parties had a chance to review them. On June 15th, 1992, the government minutes note explicitly that it had considered the minutes of the earlier Presidency meeting and then directed the relevant ministers to prepare proposals accordingly. Similarly, on 13 July, 1992, the Presidency concluded that it was necessary to estimate and make a plan for manpower regarding required for civilian functions. That was one conclusion. And another conclusion that the reserve police should be placed under the central military command. So July 13th, the Presidency reached certain conclusions as reflected in the minutes. And then we see in the minutes of July 22nd, 1992, a little over a week later, of the government on the agenda, in this case in item 11, is another explicit reference to the minutes of the Presidency. So agenda item 11 of that government session held on July 22nd states that it will address the obligations that result from the minutes of the Serb republic of BH Presidency, and then if we -- if one turns to the actual agenda item of that government session it can be seen that those particular -- that particular item is directed to an estimate of manpower available for civil needs and the issue of placing reserve police under central military command, the exact conclusions reached by the Presidency session in the minutes of July 13th. So those are a couple of examples, Mrs. Plavsic, that would seem to indicate that the minutes were taken contemporaneously, made available to the government and the government acted on those. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have in your possession minutes of the Presidency and minutes from government sessions, while in fact before I came here I had not seen a single minutes of a Presidency meeting. I have now in my possession, I don't know how many exactly, maybe 20, maybe more, but certainly not less, minutes of Presidency meetings that somebody from the Office of the Prosecutor had sent to me, including some minutes of Assembly sessions. That helped me a lot to reconstruct the dates, the time line for the purposes of writing my book, and I was really studious in reviewing this. Sometimes my memory fails me, of course, because these things happened 14 years ago and I am 76. But it was interesting to review all that, and I know that I never received minutes. I remember that I insisted, just as others did, but for instance Mr. Krajisnik is the type of man who normally likes all the formal requirements to be met, more so than Mr. Koljevic, but I remember receiving that answer from Mr. Karadzic who said, "I dictate those minutes after the session," and really from what I saw, from what I reviewed, I see that it was dictated after the event. I'm not saying that it was years later, but after the meeting is over he probably said to his secretary, "Let me dictate to you the minutes." You have those minutes, and you can see that a meeting that took two or three hours was summarised on one page observing a certain form. The meeting began at such-and-such an hour. It's usually early in the morning in the minutes, which is ridiculous to anybody who knows Mr. Karadzic. Then several items are listed, conclusions, and a signature at the bottom. Do you have such minutes? That's what I have. And I saw them for the first time when I arrived here, just as many other documents. My knowledge of all those things, if you compare what I knew before I came here with what I learnt here, the ratio would be 80 to 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, just to note that you made an observation about minutes that reflect the commencement of the Presidency session, and I simply wanted to note that somewhat consistent with what you've said about the increasingly late starting times, the minutes appear to reflect from at least mid-June onwards commencement times that begin in late morning or even early afternoon, which -- which would seem to be at least some reflection in the minutes of what you've just said about the erratic or later starting times. Do you recall that from your review of the minutes?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, you could see here and there that some meetings started even in the evening. There are things that I believe are not really relevant to this Tribunal, but somehow your question brought this up, so let me tell you. At the time when the session should have long been under way, we were still waiting and waiting, and I was the one who would make repeated calls, and Mrs. Karadzic would answer, "Radovan is sleeping." I found that point in the book of General Rose. So that's not something that is only my impression. It is shared by the representatives of the international community. Maybe that was due to his biological rhythm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we often told him you decide when the meeting will begin, and he'd say 11.00 or 12.00 and still be late. I don't think it's really very important, but your question brought it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... pressing you for more details on that point. Mrs. Plavsic, I assured you and the Court at the beginning of this session that I would be brief, and I will comply with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I've concluded these questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And thank you, Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you want to start questioning Ms. Plavsic or would there be anything else you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I do and very shortly, Your Honour, but I just also wish to seek guidance yet again. Mr. Tieger has -- if we leave aside the bit about the translation, which is probably fair to do, Mr. Tieger's taken 28 minutes by our calculation as against his allowance of an hour and 20 minutes. Is it now, and it's a reasonable question to ask, Your Honour, is it now in mind the Prosecution that they have kept back 50 minutes for further cross-examination following the Defence's cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the Court is looking at me so I presume they want my response about that. And the answer would be: Yes, I think that precisely is implied with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. I think I have intervene here. Mr. Tieger, I said within certain limits. I mean, if you would have questioned Mrs. Plavsic for ten minutes and then thought that the remainder of one hour and ten minutes would be yours, then you would have changed the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I don't mean to interrupt. I'm not trying to impose some schedule on the Court by any means with that response. I'm simply -- whatever -- if questions arise later and the Prosecution thinks it's proper to raise and useful to the Court to raise additional questions, we'll make that known. Whatever those questions might be, we understood they'd have to fit within the overall allotted time whether or not there will be such questions or how long they might take of course I leave to the Court, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means, Mr. Stewart, of course, the Chamber has considered the different scenarios, and therefore I gave the example at the beginning that if you'd use one hour, 20 minutes would remain. Of course the Chamber did not have in mind if you start with ten minutes then one hour and ten minutes would remain because that would actually change the order. At the same time, it is not the usual examination-in-chief, cross-examination situation was we often found -- find it. Let's see. Let's see how it goes and whether it would be fair if Mr. Tieger -- let's also listen to his questions and we might well say there's less time left, because you have changed the basic idea underlying the procedure for Chamber witnesses, that is, that Prosecution put questions to the witness as the first party after the Bench and then the Defence. I think it's clear. Mr. Tieger, this also means that if out of technical reasons you thought it would be wise to keep most of the time reserved for later -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, I raised this matter with Mr. Stewart yesterday. It's not a tactical issue by any means. If the Court -- and we fully endorse this approach. If the Court determines the questions raised appear to be even inadvertently a circumvention of the normal order rather than the -- the Court will act accordingly. So we understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The basics are more or less clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm afraid they're not, Your Honour. It's true Mr. Tieger raised now I can discuss it raised with me informally after court this matter but in the sense that he assured me that his request yesterday that there might be further examination by the Prosecution after our cross-examination was not just a tactical or procedural manoeuvre but, Your Honour, that's quite a different thing from that we have now in the light of the timing laid down by the Court because essentially this is a change of the order. And may I, Your Honour, indicate where this leaves the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not know that yet, Mr. Stewart, because it might be there are no further questions [indiscernible] later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say where this puts --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I beg your pardon. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, also keeping in the back of our mind the Chamber would like to avoid that we -- that the time available for putting questions to the witness would be consumed by the discussion on how we would use that time and then have no time left for -- for putting questions to the witness which is, of course, most important to do today, you're invited to start your examination of Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I simply cannot with respect be prevented from making submissions on this matter, and the importance of asking questions of the witness doesn't seem to be very great bearing in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you've got two minutes to further -- make further submissions on the matter and then the Chamber will decide whether we'll proceed according -- in accordance with what I just said or whether there will be any change. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence is in this position: We do not know now whether we are to cross-examine and stop within our time and then if we stop within our time we do not know whether the time that we have reserved is only then to be used for questions which in some way arise out of the Prosecution's further questions or whether we are then able to complete our cross-examination. Your Honour -- Your Honour has given me two minutes. What the Prosecution have done is so near to the situation that Your Honour hypothesised of stopping after ten minutes as to make no practical difference. When we look at the very, very thin ground that's actually been covered in about 20 minutes, that is in effect what has happened. They have given up over about an hour of their time. This is in our submission, Your Honour, a real, substantial reversal and interference with not just the normal order but what Your Honours had in mind as the order. This really is not acceptable, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will determine on the basis of what happens who has still time for what. It's not fair to assume, and it's clearly contradicted by Mr. Tieger that this was a tactical approach. Neither could one exclude that the results would be more or less what it would have been if it would have been a tactical approach. Rather than discussing this for another time, Mr. Stewart, the Chamber would like to proceed, as I said before. So you're invited to put questions to Mrs. Plavsic. And if time would be left at the very end, and if the parties would then ask to use that time by putting additional questions to the witness, the Chamber will consider that, and then irrespective or whether -- and we would see then in what situation we are whether that would be a clear cross-examination or examination situation where you would be allowed to address additional matters, we'll determine that at the point in time where the matter becomes actual.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I ask for guidance, please, Your Honour. If I -- if I were to use my entire allocation, I'm then in the Court's hands as to discretion as to whether I get further time. And if I don't use the whole of my allocation, am I in the same position, that I'm not guaranteed getting the balance ultimately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're trying to get the best out of the presence of Mrs. Plavsic who was called on behalf of the Chamber. If you would not have used the whole of the time allocated to you and if further time would remain, then we would certainly consider how to use that time, and I certainly do not exclude that additional time might be given for new matters to be addressed in the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will -- I will proceed, Your Honour, but I will also, please, Your Honour has invited me not to take more time on this, but I would reserve the Defence's position entirely in relation to all these matters that have come up, and they are also the matter that we would also want to take with discussing at Mr. Krajisnik at some point, but, Your Honour, with that express reservation yes indeed then I will as Your Honour asks me to do, proceed with examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Plavsic, questions will now be put to you by Mr. Stewart who is the Defence counsel for Mr. Krajisnik. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I don't know if there are a lot of microphones on. I'm getting a great -- maybe it's something this morning. I'm getting a great deal of interference from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is some. I do agree. The attention of the technicians is asked for the problem. There is some interference. It's for me not at such a level, but.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may also be a computer that makes a bit of noise. If we find the source, please remove the source; if not, the level is such that we can continue at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's like that but we'll crack on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- Mrs. Plavsic, good morning?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say in your statement and you describe in your evidence people coming to visit Mr. Krajisnik in Pale, and you said that his office was always full of people because deputies and municipal authorities from different regions would report to him about various regional problems. How often from the point when you arrived in Pale in late May, 1992, how often did you see this?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deal with that. I didn't follow it. I had no such intent. It's just the impression that I gained, and when one gains an impression it implies that it's something that recurred over those months many times. It was a usual thing to meet somebody, to run into somebody who would tell you, "I'm going up there to see Krajisnik. I'm going up there to -- because I need Krajisnik." And in the anteroom where his secretary sat, there were always many people who would be waiting to go in. That's something that I observed. And generally speaking, Mr. Krajisnik, as president of the Assembly, certainly had to have contacts with Assembly men as part of his work. As for municipal authorities, I don't know whether his contacts with them followed from some tasks he got from the party. I don't know what his tasks within the party were. I know that he was a well-respected man within the party. And as for the economy, I know he was considered as very competent, very expert. He was a member of I don't know how many professional boards or technical boards. And when I said he was a powerful man, I did not mean anything negative. I just noted a fact, that power, and I believe I spoke about that yesterday, transpired from various ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, whatever criticisms you might make and we know do make of Mr. Krajisnik, you would agree, wouldn't you, that he is -- he is a man who was always receptive to listening to the problems of others and doing what he could to help?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend those meetings. I wasn't there. But if some people constantly go to see a man, well, they wouldn't be going to see somebody who is totally unable to, let me not say fulfil their wishes, but provide whatever they needed. Sometimes it was the very basic necessities that these people were lacking, something indispensable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But my question was a little bit -- a little bit general, Mrs. Plavsic. Leaving aside these particular meetings, as your general experience of Mr. Krajisnik, would you agree that he was somebody who was always receptive to listening to the problems of others and anxious to do what he could to help?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. People would probably not have gone to him if he had been a different man. Our people would say that he is the sort of man who knows how to ask, "How are you? How's your family do?" Unlike some other people who did not have that habit because they were different by nature. Let me give you an example. In Sarajevo, I was unable for a while to run away. I was with my mother, who was 85 at the time and totally immobile. Mr. Karadzic never called to say, "How are you managing in this situation?" Whereas Mr. Krajisnik did. He would just ask people how they were doing, if they needed anything, and that's probably why people went to see him. And they were thinking something like, I'm going to see Krajisnik. I'll probably find some support and assistance there. But I don't know. I didn't see with my own eyes either what they asked for or what they got, but good communication from the local people on his part, because communication lines with the local level were very poor. The corridor from the eastern part to the western part was blocked for a while, and you had to take a roundabout macadam road, travel under very difficult conditions, sometimes under gunfire. The line was a thousand and 700 kilometres long. People would sometimes come to see him because they needed something undergoing many difficulties on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mrs. Plavsic your answer in fact contains the answer to my next three questions so if we continue in this telepathic way we will use the time very well indeed. Mrs. Plavsic, did you have any knowledge in May, June, July, 1992, of any visits by Mr. Krajisnik to other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any particular information. Maybe it was like that. I don't know. I mean, I wasn't really following what Mr. Krajisnik was doing. I didn't always know when he was in his office all the time. I just didn't follow that. But there were times when I looked for him and he wasn't there, and then his secretary would say, "The president has gone to such-and-such a place." That's how I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, let me make it clear. Nobody I think, but certainly not I am urging you to speculate. Just to be clear, then, did Mr. Krajisnik, in 1992, let's stay with that year, did he ever accompany you, with or without any other people, on any visit to any other municipality?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It seems to me that we did go to a meeting together that had to do with the airport, but it's possible that that wasn't. So either someone was with me, however, they didn't travel with me. When I say "travel" it might sound silly when applied to an hour-long trip by car, but when the topic of surrendering the airport to the UNPROFOR was being dealt with, I think that I did describe that event in my book by saying that I thought that -- that Mr. Krajisnik also attended that meeting, but I wasn't definite about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- do you have any recollection at all that you might, in 1992, have gone with Mr. Krajisnik, with or without anybody else, to any municipality outside the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember. When I came to Pale, I was in Pale the entire time. There was just one invitation from November sad to appear on their television and I went. Otherwise, I was thought of as somebody who sat house, quote unquote, who was there looking after the house where we were staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, during 1992 did you report directly to Mr. Krajisnik following any visit or contact by you with any municipality outside the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall going outside of the Sarajevo municipality. You are taking into account the period from late May until the end of 1992. Is that the period that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We probably ought to just make that clearer. It's my fault, Mrs. Plavsic, for not being sufficiently specific. I am talking about whole of 1992, not just from May. So I am included the period when you were still in Sarajevo and you were still for the early part of that year a member of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency. So with that clarification, could you deal with the broader question then for 1992? Just to remind you, did you ever report directly to Mr. Krajisnik following a visit by you in 1992 to any municipality outside the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First let me say I don't know how you imagine this report to be. At the time, I was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I was elected at the first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina together with Mr. Koljevic to represent the Serbian people. I was not obliged to report to or to inform Mr. Krajisnik of any matters by nature of my post. I informed the Presidency whose member I was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About my activities. This has to do with your term reporting. I think that has a sort of official tone. But as to whether I met Mr. Krajisnik, I don't mean on the street but sort of encountered him in a conversation, perhaps, "Biljana, I haven't seen you. Did you go anywhere?" And then I would answer "yes, to such-and-such a place," and it would be a conversation. But you have to remind you of that. As to reporting, I was only obliged to report to the Presidency, and I did report to them. So you have to be specific and tell me what this exactly this is about and which period it covers. The 8th of April was the last day of my Presidency membership. This was 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's being taken care of. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Plavsic, you're addressing Mr. Stewart, which is fine, but the interpreters have some difficulty in catching your voice from the microphone. So the one microphone to be turned a bit. So if you please keep in mind that they should be able to hear you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Plavsic, I'll try to -- to it clarify then. It's possible that the word I'm using in English, of report, is having some stronger, official meaning. When I'm talking and asking whether you reported to Mr. Krajisnik or anybody else, we can take it for the rest of the morning or however long I have of the morning that I'm not confining it to that sort of official report. I'm talking about simply telling him or telling somebody what happened, that sort of reporting. Does that -- does that help if I add that clarification?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't help me. Please tell me specifically and I will tell you yes or no directly. I mean, you need to be more specific, otherwise I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll build it into the specific questions, then, Mrs. Plavsic. We'll do it that way. Did you -- whether or not you had any sort of official obligation to do it and in whatever formal or informal manner it was done, did you at any time in 1992 report to Mr. Krajisnik following any visit or contact by you to or with a municipality outside the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not obliged to report or inform Mr. Krajisnik. If I had been a member of any body within the SDS, and Mr. Krajisnik did have a post in the SDS and if you were to ask me which ones, I know that he was just not a regular member of the SDS like I was. So had I had some post there, maybe in accordance with that hierarchy I would have been duty-bound to report to him. In this way, I wasn't. If you're talking about the period when I was a member of the Presidency, the Presidency sent me to several places. I often thought I was the only woman there and they were sending me somewhere where a stronger man would need to be sent, but it wasn't my habit to refuse work, and it wasn't my habit to protect myself. If we're talking about that period, I only reported to the Presidency. Wherever I would go, the media would go with me. What would happen could be seen on the news the next day, where the member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was. She was sent there because of such-and-such a thing, and her report says such-and-such. It was all public. TV cameras would follow the events. I would be visiting these areas as a member of the Presidency. I would never go alone. Either somebody else from the Presidency would go with me or from the government. As far as I can recall, there was never anyone from the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and discussions were held at that level. The Presidency did not see it, and I don't recall that anything that was discussed there would be confidential or secret. All was discussed usually in the presence of journalists, and I saw no reason for the secrecy. So if you are interested in something specific, I would like you to be specific then, which date, what was my post at the time, and I will tell you right away. At the time when I was a member of the Presidency, the Presidency was the -- actually, the Assembly was the highest legislative body, but according to a kind of hierarchy the Presidency was above the Assembly. Well, I really cannot present to you what the relations were. I'm not even thinking about that any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll try as best I can to follow your request to make my questions specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- in our submission, the -- that answer clearly, implicitly contains a straight no to my question. If the Trial Chamber or the Prosecutor suggests anything different, then I would perhaps have to pursue it different, but in my submission it does contain a clear no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could clarify then one detail. Let me try to do it. Mrs. Plavsic, you said whenever you were sent somewhere cameras would follow you, everything was in the open, you had no duty to report to Mr. Krajisnik or the Assembly. At the same time, in one of your earlier answers you said something that, "I would see him. I would say to him, well, I went there and then, and had a brief conversation on it." Does your last extensive answer on reporting change what you said earlier, or would you say, "Well, all the reporting, cameras, et cetera, that was there at such level I did not speak about the matters with Mr. Krajisnik, but we might have had just an informal conversation when we met. Not a scheduled meeting but just when I would see him, I would say, Yesterday I went there." Would apart from where your answer seems to clearly say no formal report, and you set out what the situation was, would that -- would you say, "I nevertheless might have had this type of informal conversation with him," as I described before? I mean, did the two be next to each other or did one exclude the other?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to know again if this refers to the period when I was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was clearly understood, and I understand your answer to be that it was mainly at that period in time when you were sent somewhere. So it certainly would be included.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who sent me? I would go wherever the Presidency would send me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear, Mrs. Plavsic, but I just wanted to hear from you where you said, no formal reporting, these were official visits, et cetera. So at that level I never reported to Mr. Krajisnik. But would that -- would it still have been possible that when seeing him in passing that you had a brief conversation? "Yesterday, I went there and there," and so just informal chat?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me. Excuse me, Mrs. Plavsic. The exchange at page 30, line 11, where Mrs. Plavsic quite fairly asked for clarification again, I would like to know again if this refers to the period when I was a member in BiH, Your Honour said that was clearly understood. Your Honour, I had tried to make it clear to Mrs. Plavsic that in fact it was the precise opposite and that my questions did relate to the whole of 1992 and that is going to confuse the issue enormously in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact that I said then -- let me just find it again. I later said it would certainly be included, and that would mean that includes the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That doesn't resolve the ambiguity and confusion, Your Honour, one bit. Well, Your Honour -- it's Your Honour's questions at the moment, but I'm just saying if Your Honour's -- if Your Honour's questions then proceed on a different basis from my questions then the witness will get terribly confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. I then leave it in your hands. I just wanted to find out -- I take it that that was clear to you. I just wanted to find out whether the answer clearly indicated that there was in no way any formal reporting on any of those visits whether still occasional conversations of a total informal character would take place and if there's any ambiguity in time you're invited to -- to clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mrs. Plavsic, I tried to make it clear that my question was not confined to formal reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So forgive me one moment, Your Honour. I'm having to disentangle some questions and points here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you recall in the whole of 1992 any informal reporting by you in whatever way, however casual, to Mr. Krajisnik following any visit or contact with you -- by you with a municipality outside the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that in this way you would not be able to disentangle anything. If I may be allowed to say something that you have tangled up. The only way to say it is to say it in that and that period you were in such-and-such a place. Did you inform Mr. Krajisnik about that or not? The year of 1992 was completely different. Early 1992 until, let's say April 8th, and then there April 8th onwards. These were two completely different environments. There was peace such as it was. It was a little tense. It was bringing in some ugly signals, but then after that the war came. And I can reply to a well-formulated question, but believe me, I agree that it is all tangled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when something is tangled, I would not be able to. I don't know how to come out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm going to get my disentangling tools ready again, Mrs. Plavsic. And have another go. Let's do it this way, I hope this will help you: Up to the time when you resigned from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 8th, I think it was, of April, 1992, we know that a few days previously to that you had visited Bijeljina. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone knows that. Even people abroad know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had you, in 1992, up to the 8th of April, had you visited any other municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina outside the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. I think that the day before or yesterday I said, and I saw here that there are subtitles here, not just numbers -- subheadings here, not just numbers, and I think -- and I'm talking about the summary, and it's from April. And I think that I said why from April, when there was a visit three or four days -- actually, there was a visit in late March which was very important but it's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in that case tell us, Mrs. Plavsic, please, to where was that very important visit in late March?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That visit was on the 28th of March. It was a visit to Bosanski Brod. Is that what you wanted it hear?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's going in the right direction, absolutely, Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm going to now --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then you should have asked me right away, because I'm afraid to say something because His Honour might then say that it's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... as I was, Mrs. Plavsic, but I do my best to try to be on the ball.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, let me say the following: If Mr. Stewart is putting the questions in the way he does, he gives you an opportunity to come up with your own knowledge without Mr. Stewart already suggesting something. If you ask someone, "How did you come to this Tribunal," then it's up for you to say, "I came by bicycle, by car, by plane." If you say, "Did you come by car to this Tribunal," then there is already some suggestion in it that it may well have been by car. And I think Mr. Stewart by putting his questions in this way leaves -- gives you the opportunity to come up as best as possible with your own answers and not suggesting too much. I think that might be in the back of his mind, and therefore that's fully accepted and would -- is even, I would say, quite fair to you, not to push you in a certain direction. Apart from that, Ms. Plavsic, we usually have a break at this point in time. May I ask you, did you have a chance to review the corrected version of your statement yesterday or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with the way it has been changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to look at it again. I think, as far as the terminology's concerned, the latest version still has some of the official names -- sorry, unofficial names in it. But as for substantial errors that change the meaning, they have all been corrected. I just want to tell that you without disentangling things further, it has been my problem forever, I can only answer directly if asked a direct question. I am not the kind of person who will take offence at direct questions. It is my nature but also the nature of the job that I had. I think that would facilitate things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Stewart takes your last remark on board. I suggest to the parties the following as far as the official terminology is concerned. It seems not to be a core issue. I would like to invite Mrs. Plavsic to just make circles around any terminology where -- just for the terminology she makes a reservation as to what in that respect her statement is fully correct and then ask her to sign the statement. Mrs. Plavsic, would you be so kind to read, perhaps during the next break, the statement again and just make a circle around any name of a body, et cetera, where you say, "I do not fully accept that this is the correct name," so that we know what reservation you made. We then -- this is then on the record. This is on the official record of the Tribunal that you made that reservation. It's visible in your statement, and we then ask you to initial every page of the statement and sign it. Perhaps I have one further remark to make for the parties rather in the absence of the witness. Could I invite the security to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll -- yes. Rather than having a very abstract discussion on how much time would be left, et cetera, et cetera, Mr. Tieger, could you inform us on the basis of the questions that were put to Mrs. Plavsic until now, what amount of time would that trigger for you -- so we can make an assessment. We're monitoring what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So far so helpful, Your Honour. That's a most helpful answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I might ask a similar question during the course of the further examination this witness, and of course the first issue is whether you have any questions, and then the second matter would be how much time you would need to deal with the issue you'd like to raise. And, Mr. Tieger, I think it goes without saying that if you would have one question where for many witnesses you would make that two minutes, you'll have the experience, as we have it now, it's your assessment on how much time it would take to deal with the matter you have on your mind, and don't tell me later on that you're surprised that it took more than you thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, in the hope to be helpful, I'm going to narrow down the time frame just a bit and invite you, please, to disregard January and February, 1992, so that when I'm asking from now on we can start at the beginning of March, 1992. You've told the Trial Chamber -- we know that you went to Bijeljina. That's in your statement. You've told the Trial Chamber that you went to Bosanski Brod. Did you -- from the beginning of March up to the 8th of April, did you go to any other municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina outside the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went on instructions from the Presidency to Novi Travnik, to Capljina, Kupres, Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, you said Bosanski Brod before. Is that -- that completes the list. And those five municipalities, Bosanski Brod, Novi Travnik, Capljina and Kupres that was best in that period from the beginning of March to 8th of April, in that five-week period, was it?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there -- I'll leave Bijeljina on the one side for the moment. Was your visit to Bosanski Brod in any way connected with any outbreak or reports of outbreak of violence?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the violence in Bosnia and Herzegovina started precisely in that territory, in that area, in Bosanski Brod, just after the beginning of March. The 108th Brigade crossed over from Croatia to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to our territory, and we received that report in the Presidency. The president of the Presidency did not attach particular importance to certain reports. He was somehow selective about that. But I know that on this occasion he said that we should check whether the report was correct, and how could it be checked. Somebody from the Presidency should go there. And I was chosen to go there with Mr. Abdic and Mr. Boras.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, forgive me if I may seem to be cutting you off. I just at the moment rather than going into the details in these particular municipalities, I'm just trying to check through them. Again, a brief answer, please. Was your visit to Novi Travnik linked to any outbreak of violence there or reports of outbreak of violence there? And I'm seeking a pretty near to a yes or no answer, Mrs. Plavsic, with respect.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer, because what I consider violence, and there was violence, is when barracks containing conscripts are cut off from their supply of electricity, water, and food, and all that is decided not by the Presidency but by the local community. I went there with Mr. Doko, the minister of defence, who is a Croat. Capljina is a Croat area, meaning that it is populated mostly by Croats. And there was somebody from the police, I believe Mr. -- somebody from the police. Somebody that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic insisted should go. And I, the member of Presidency, was asking and begging and reminding people from the local community that those people should have water to drink and food to eat, nothing more than that, and they did not allow it. In the same way, other barracks were surrounded and cut off, and that was an assault on the army of Yugoslavia that was still a regular army. In order to achieve something in that type of situation, I had to beg people, to remind them that they had children, too, that those children are also serving in the army or may be serving in the army, and could they imagine what it would be like if their children had no electricity and no food and no water. And I didn't meet with much support, although I had some support from Mr. Doko.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, can I just try to tie together straight away Capljina and Kupres just in this way: Is it also correct, just keeping your answer to this point, please, that your visits to both Capljina and Kupres were connected with violence or hostilities or reports of violence or hostilities?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My visits were attempts to defuse that situation; unfortunately, I failed. Not only I, because I was not alone from the Presidency who went there, and we did not manage, unfortunately, to lift the blockade of the barracks in Capljina. We did not manage to save the Serbs from the massacre they experienced in Kupres just after we left. Mr. Boras has the best intentions, and although he had separate talks with the Croats, I do not doubt that he advised them not to do such things, but the troops were coming from Tomislavgrad, formerly called Duvno, and he had to go there and I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Plavsic. I'd like to look specifically at your visit to Bijeljina on the 4th of April, 1992. Do you have a copy of your -- your statement as it now stands in your own language there with you? If not, then -- you do. You have it in front of you. Excellent. Could you look, please, then to paragraph 13 which is under the heading "Visit to Bijeljina on 4th of April, 1992." Do you find that point? If -- I'm sure Their Honours would agree, Mrs. Plavsic, that if at any point you need time to refresh yourself as to what you said or to be clear, I believe you only have to ask. The -- you -- paragraph 14, you say -- well, you say around the 7th it of April you were contacted and so on, and then paragraph 14 you were instructed by the president to go to Bijeljina, and Mr. Izetbegovic stated that the minority Muslim population in the municipality were in a dangerous situation and that there had been massacres of Muslims there. You describe, and I'm not dwelling on this in detail then, but nor do I wish to rush you through it, you describe what you saw, broken windows. You understood there had been fighting, young men in blue uniform. You refer to Arkan, visits to Muslim families. Paragraph 19, you didn't see any dead bodies, but you say you did talk to some people whose family members had been killed during the fighting. And then going to -- you talk about the Serb flag being hoisted on the mosque and then paragraph 22 which is the conclusion of this passage, your statement, you say, "When we returned, Mr. Abdic and I gave a very short oral report to the Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency. My report was that nothing out of the ordinary had happened in Bijeljina." Mrs. Plavsic, I want to clarify with you. First of all, compared with ordinary life in Bijeljina in peacetime, it was absolutely obvious that what had happened there was out of the ordinary, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the reason why I went there. If the situation had been normal, there would have been no reason to go there. Mr. Izetbegovic had read a report that a massacre of Muslims in Bijeljina had already been committed or was in preparation. I remember that very well. And at that Presidency session, I said it's impossible. Bijeljina is not some backwater village so that we could not know about it. It's not so far from Sarajevo that we wouldn't hear news from there. But that was my spontaneous reaction, especially in view of the fact that two hours prior to that I talked to Mr. Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hope you won't consider it rude. Such interruptions normally are rather rude, but I only have very limited time, and I really am going to quite formally invite you to stick to the questions I'm asking and concentrate on answering them. The -- the point is this: That -- do you agree, just to get some clear guidelines, to say that nothing out of the ordinary had happened in Bijeljina as a general, simple proposition literally stated like that is obviously absurd, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who said that nothing happened in Bijeljina? It happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic -- Mrs. Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The massacre didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Bear with me, Mrs. Plavsic. Your statement to this Court is saying that your report in 1992 back to the Presidency was that nothing out of ordinary had happened in Bijeljina, and I'm just putting to you that stated in that simple way that's obviously absurd, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you taking that sentence out of context? Of course it looks that way if you do that. When somebody takes a sentence out of context, we call it manipulation, although I'm not saying that you are manipulating. Of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to you then is to put it in context. You're the witness. This is your statement. This is what you're saying about your report. I'm only asking the question. So please put it in context as much as you wish to do to make the point clear. It's an open invitation for you to put it in context.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic said that a massacre had happened in Bijeljina. That's what he said at a Presidency session. At that Presidency session, that morning, early that morning, Mr. Abdic came and he was sitting there, and at that moment he said, "That's not true, Alija. It's true I was captured there, but there was no massacre." And I only expressed doubt to that one claim. And Mr. Izetbegovic responded by saying, "Mrs. Plavsic, if you have any doubts, why don't you go and see for yourself?" I replied that I won't go unless the Presidency ordered me to do so and I'm not going alone. So some other people were appointed including General Prascevic who was travelling in other car and Mr. Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, let's look at your --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 2nd military districts General Prascevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, let's look at your statement. Paragraph 15 when you arrived in Bijeljina no people on the streets you got the impression that the town was empty. Was that an ordinary situation for Bijeljina? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you that something happened. You are constantly trying to put it to me that I had said that nothing had happened in Bijeljina. It did. The observation that I made that streets were empty in itself is something out of the ordinary from a normally busy town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shop windows about shattered. That's also not normal. It was obvious that something had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can -- we can -- Mrs. --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even here and there you could hear shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can shorten this, I feel confident.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, shorten it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you in fact report with no significant qualification to the Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency that nothing out of the ordinary had happened in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. It was a verbal report just after I came back, but not only to the Presidency. We travelled actually via Tuzla, and in Tuzla there was a press conference where I shared my impressions as to what had happened, and Mr. Abdic did the same. It seemed very odd to me, though, that he was giving his briefing in one room and I was giving my briefing in another room, and both of us protested against that because we were both members of the same body, and we could sit together and brief the public. However, when I saw that, I realised what was going on. That morning, in the mass media, only my statements were related, not those of Mr. Abdic. Maybe -- Mr. Abdic is a very vain man. He burst into my office and said, "This is pure impudence that my voice is not heard at all, and nothing of what I said to the media is reported." I told him, "Abdic, go and ask Izetbegovic. Don't you see what kind of game this is?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Plavsic, the question is this: With the context that we see in your statement, your statement nevertheless in the second sentence of paragraph 22 does say that your report was that nothing out of the ordinary had happened in Bijeljina, and it seems to be, Mrs. Plavsic, that for whatever reason, pressures or whatever, that sentence is not accurate and does require significant qualification. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what you just said is not in paragraph 22. I'll read it. It's a very brief paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you allow me?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, of course.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "When we returned, Mr. Abdic and I gave just a very brief verbal report to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that report, I did not mention the Serb flag hoisted on the mosque in Bijeljina. A few days later, we were supposed -- I was supposed to submit a written report. However, on the 8th of April, I resigned from my position in the Presidency. I believe that Mr. Krajisnik was not informed about my visit to Bijeljina." All this stands. If I did not mention the flag on the mosque, how can you conclude that I said that nothing happened in Bijeljina? I believe that the flag on top of the mosque, from a moral point of view, if I can call it that, it was out of place. And I discussed it with Abdic. And I told others, why did they put up that flag on the mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note this sentence is missing in the Serbian translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Either let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mrs. Plavsic, please. We have to sort something out. The interpreters have raised something which has already become, I think, very clear, certainly to His Honours -- I think I -- to Their Honours, I can see, and to me, which is that a sentence which I have in front of me absolutely clearly in black and white in the English version appears to have gone missing in some way from the Serb version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mrs. Plavsic reading out that paragraph, there was no equivalent of the second sentence that we're seeing in the English version, unless I am completely mishearing or misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a -- there seems to be a problem as far as translation is concerned. When you were invited to read, Mrs. Plavsic, you read from the -- what we call B/C/S, that's Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian version, and it seems that one line from the English has not been translated, I tell you, and that caused all of the problem. There is one line in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] I can see because now I'm comparing that. It's awful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, how awful it is, of course --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's awful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course we could look back both in the audio, but let's just clarify then that you say, "This is not what I told the Presidency, that nothing out of the ordinary had happened in Bijeljina." I suggest to the parties, given the -- given the clarifications given by Mrs. Plavsic about the report that we strike this from the statement as -- of course, the parties will have an opportunity to -- to look in the transcript and the audio of the original so that we know, but for the time being the type of reporting seems to be better understood without this sentence than with this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, that's absolutely right with respect as far as it goes, but it leaves some matters. Your Honour, I have a couple of submissions which really would be better made in the absence of Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Plavsic, since you, from what we now know you understand English quite well, Mr. Stewart wanted to raise a procedural issue which he'd rather do in your absence, that is not to influence you in any way and you not -- so you could please for a second leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all there's if you like the practical technical aspect and then there's what flows from it. Our understanding had been that, and we think this is right, that Mrs. Plavsic's interview in Sweden, being entirely conducted in English, the statement prepared by the Trial Chamber was, of course, prepared in English, and then at the final stages, before it was sent to Mrs. Plavsic in Sweden it was translated from English into her language so that the -- that sentence in the English statement which was, if you like, the statement, disappeared in some way from the Serbian. There was then -- and these things happen, but it was not picked up when Mrs. Plavsic checked her statement, made amendments. It was subsequently never picked up that that sentence hadn't appeared in her version, so we continued with the version in English.
