But, Your Honour, the problem is not merely a technical one because this is most unfortunate, because I have conducted the last 15 or 20 minutes of cross-examination entirely reasonably, I don't believe anybody could suggest anything different, entirely reasonably on the footing that that was a sentence in Mrs. Plavsic's statement and that's what she was saying. And it's worse, Your Honours, because Your Honours will have seen that over the last 15 or 20 minutes, I have, as counsel often do, I have changed my tone of cross-examination. We do. That's what we do. That's part of our job. And my tone of cross-examination in relation to Mrs. Plavsic has changed to a considerable result as a consequence of her answers which are not surprisingly slightly -- getting slightly heated and frustrated on her part for reasons which I could not understand because I now see why that was so. So this has significantly altered the thrust and the dynamics, if you like, and the tone of my cross-examination of Mrs. Plavsic as a result of a completely false basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you suggest to -- we have -- Mr. Stewart, we have all experienced over the last years in this trial that sometimes human failure in translating and in many other respects negatively impacted on what we are doing. We have lost time. We have done things we would not have done if such human failure would not have been there. It cannot be otherwise for such a long period of time, but of course we should try to keep it to the bear minimum which could be achieved at normal human standards. This Chamber, whether it was about translation or any other matter, always has tried to repair as good as it could such human failure. What your suggestion at this moment for repair of -- I do agree with you, a very unfortunate situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Two things, Your Honour. First of all, of course human -- we're all human. I don't quarrel with that at all, Your Honour. Of course we have to accept that, naturally. The possibility of human error is always slightly aggravated by what we have submitted already, Your Honour, is the accelerated pace of some of these matters. But we are where we are now, Your Honour. First of all this is sufficiently disconcerting that we really do wish, however quickly it can be done, we do wish an immediate checking to make sure that there is no other such error or deficiency. It shouldn't take very long, Your Honour, but that really needs to be done, because, with respect, I do not wish to have a repetition of this sort of problem in my approach to cross-examination. Secondly, Your Honour, some of the -- whether it's damage or whatever, it's not that I would have chosen to do if I had known the correct position about 20, 25 minutes ago, I would invite Your Honour, not me, I would invite Your Honour to give Mrs. Plavsic a -- please, a very clear indication that there has been an error for which and in this particular case, Your Honour, I'm going to have to ask that it is made crystal clear that it is no fault whatever of the Defence and that we have been put at a disadvantage by a human error -- I don't mind that -- we have been put at a disadvantage and Mrs. Plavsic should understand that the Defence has operated under a considerable difficulty over the last half hour as a result of an error and misunderstanding in relation to her statement. That, we submit, is fair as a corrective measure in relation to the Defence and the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the brief answer would have been whether this Chamber is willing to take action so that the translation is checked. That's one. And second, to explain to Mrs. Plavsic what happened and that -- that the Defence took the course based on an unfortunate --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, my answer is my answer, Your Honour, brief or not. That's what I'm inviting Your Honour please to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My suggestion is that your answers are a bit more brief but let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours always makes that suggestion, always, always makes that suggestion; whether it advances the case one doesn't really always know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've still not given up the hope that you once understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I dare say not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Could Mrs. Plavsic be brought into the courtroom again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- sorry. I was only going to suggest that we then build in the actual signing of the statement at the appropriate time in the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, we found ourselves in the very unfortunate situation, as you have found out by yourself now as well, that one line in the English did not appear in the copy on which you most likely will have focused, that is the copy in your own language. That should not have happened. I meanwhile took an initiative to have the two copies carefully compared whether everything that is in the one is in the other as well. This is not a full check of the translation as such, but at least to see that not a sentence appear in the one copy and not in the other. I took action to see whether this can be done still when we are proceeding here. Questions were put to you on that one specific line, and of course Mr. Stewart was very insisting on an explanation, on a line which did not appear in your language, and of course Mr. Stewart at that time had no idea that it was not in your language. So therefore when at a certain moment he was very insisting in this matter, and even when it took a course which you might have considered not to be the most pleasant one, certainly Mr. Stewart, who speaks perfect English but no B/C/S, is not in any way responsible for that. I just want you to know that. And then I'll invite Mr. Stewart to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My I just inform you, Your Honour I know you gave specific instructions for Mrs. Plavsic not to discuss testimony during the break. I did sit with her because she was obviously agitated. We didn't discuss the testimony but we did discuss this problem just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's -- it's appreciated that you are transparent on the matter and I think where in the beginning we said that we do not have to give you further guidance as to what your role would be. This Chamber would consider this to be within your role and I do not see any disagreement by parties in this case. Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. We continue and now, hopefully, without mistakes of this kind which should not have been there. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I say Your Honour that you 10 per cent met my concerns and my requests for which I'm extremely grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, who -- well, were, maybe are -- I'm sorry, I don't know whether it's "are," Prince and princess Karadjordjevic?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prince Tomislav Karadjordjevic is the second son of King Aleksandar Karadjordjevic who was the King of Yugoslavia before World War 2, until 1934 when he was killed in Marseilles. And after that he was supposed to have been succeeded by his oldest son Petar, and until he reached the age of 18, Yugoslavia was governed by a commissioning body. Then after World War II, the Communists came to power and the dynasty was forbidden from returning. And then in the period after the death of Tito there was a certain degree of democratisation. Certain things changed to a degree. So I don't know exactly when Prince Tomislav -- he is not the heir to the crown according to the proper succession, but he was allowed to return to Belgrade. And his wife is an Englishwoman, Princess Linda. I saw her in Frankfurt. I respect highly all the members of our dynasty. If you ask me, I am a monarchist, even though that is very far from being actually realised. But not only do I respect them for being who they are, but they are also good people. And when he had to leave the country, he was a young boy perhaps of 11 years or so, and of course he wanted to return. He died in 2000 in Belgrade. At that time, it was two and a half years that the Milosevic authorities forbade me from entering Serbia, and permits were issued so that -- even Crown Prince Aleksandar was issued a permit to come the funeral. I was issued with that kind of permit to attend the funeral and return immediately. I don't know if you need any more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What we do see -- thank you, Mrs. Plavsic. What we see from your statement was that -- at the end -- it's paragraph 23. At the end of April, 1992, the prince asked you if you would go with Princess Linda to some places in Bosnia-Herzegovina and you specifically say that you went to Foca. In a -- in a nutshell, please, if I may put it that way, Mrs. Plavsic, what was the role of -- of Prince Tomislav Karadjordjevic and Princess Linda in all this at this time?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no official role. They were members of the dynasty, patriots. They had heard -- they also had the opportunity to see and to read in the foreign press about how Serbs were committing atrocities on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I must tell you that General Morillon told me at that there was a media war being waged against Serbs. I can give you the whole sentence. "Perhaps you will win this war but, Mrs. Plavsic, you have already lost the media war." This was 1993. At that time, I did not quite understand that something like that could happen, but it did happen in this war. And I remember that General Nambiar, in his report to the Security Council said that the media, to a considerable part, contributed to the evil in Bosnia and Herzegovina. For a while, he was the UNPROFOR commander in chief in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war. To go back to Prince Tomislav Karadjordjevic and his wife, Princess Linda. He asked me is this true. I said it's impossible. "Biljana, would you go together with Linda, because she would like to see for herself." Princess Linda had a way of publishing the truth. At least she thought that she had a way of making it possible to have the truth published, even in the British parliament. In this way, the Minister of Internal Affairs at the time in Blair's government, John Reid, he actually came twice on the recommendation of Princess Linda to see for himself what was going on. But let me say something about Foca. We went early in the morning by plane and returned in the same plane that evening to Foca. There was Princess Linda, but not only her. There were many people who were bringing in humanitarian aid, mostly medicines. The hospitals were poorly supplied with medicines. We went to Foca. We talked with the municipal government. I asked them about the hospital, could we go to the hospital, and at the hospital we were given a report about the state of affairs there. We visited all the patients. I didn't and she isn't either ask who was who, whether they were Serbs, Muslims or Croats. They were all being treated equally. But I believe that it was useful because she heard that there was a shortage of antibiotics. So she focused all of her effort to tell others there were no antibiotics at the hospitals and that she also would help. She did have -- I can't say a major opportunity, but she did have a opportunity to help. She did form an impression, even though it was a brief staying from morning until the evening. When I say the evening, it doesn't mean that we were there in Foca from morning to evening. The plane flew to Podgorica. Then there was a car from Podgorica to Niksic, and then from Niksic via Pluzine to Foca. I think that the trip took a long time. The actual time spent in Foca was actually not more than a couple of hours. So for her to form an impression, it would have been necessary to stay in Foca for a few days, and then she would have been able to really perform the job that she came there to perform, but we did manage to achieve something. They did get antibiotics. The same thing happened in Foca. We returned and then Prince Tomislav said, "Do you want to go to Zvornik now?" So I also wasn't to Zvornik with Princess Linda again, and I think according to the protocol -- I didn't know anybody there. We would go to the municipal office and ask, "Could you provide me such-and-such information?" And I know in the end they told us, "If you want, you can go and visit Muslim houses and talk with their families," and that's what we did. I think that we entered four or five houses. I know exactly which houses, where we went to these houses, and we did get information. We talked not with Serbs but with Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If I may, Mrs. --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're interested in what they told us and how all of this finished, I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, first of all if I may just ask you a quick series of short questions just to get some things sorted out and then we could come back to any of these other matters as necessary. You say that you'd been asked by prince Tomislav if you could escort Princess Linda to some places in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You went to Foca. You went to Zvornik, as you described. Did you go to any other municipalities pursuant to that request from Prince Tomislav?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was that. It was a very brief period. I had to return to Sarajevo. My mother was alone, but during that time my brother was there but he couldn't stay there. I think that all together it took perhaps three days. After three days, I came back to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's very helpful, Mrs. Plavsic. I just wanted to get that clear. And then following your visits then to Foca and to Zvornik, did you and/or Princess Linda, did you then give a report to anybody? And I'm meaning any sort of report, formal, informal, official, unofficial. Did you report back to somebody?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was no longer a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina when this happened. You need to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's follow that up. This request was nothing to do with the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was it? It didn't come from them. It wasn't -- it wasn't --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was no longer a member as of the 8th of April, and this was -- it's hard to say. Perhaps in mid-April or more towards the end of April. I'm not sure. In any case, I was no longer a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the war had already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we clear this out of way then? These visits to Foca and Zvornik, they were not at the request of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were not instigated by them. You were under no obligation to report back to that Presidency and you didn't report back to that Presidency. Is that all correct? Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct. On the 8th of April I left the Presidency building and I never went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So -- so --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I never went back to the town because the town was already full of posters of Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic, and me, and on the posters there was the slogan "War criminals," so it was dangerous to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So to whom, if anybody, to whom did you and Princess Linda report what you had seen and found in Foca and Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No report to anyone. I was not in any kind of official position to submit a report to anyone. Maybe I spoke with someone and said I went with Linda there. She promised that she would bring antibiotics, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- we're talking about events from 14 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're younger than me. I don't know if you would remember things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I known that I would be in this position, I would probably have had a piece of paper with me all the time, and I would have been jotting things down just in case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mrs. Plavsic, but the -- I -- I've got to use a different word. Did you tell anybody when you returned from Foca and Zvornik, did you tell anybody the details of what you had seen and found in those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Prince Tomislav, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we returned, and in those talks with the Muslim population in their homes we found out that many people fled to Loznica, across the bridge, that they got frightened. Loznica is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you tell --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I -- I was not -- I had to return to Sarajevo to care for my mother, so I was not able to. And then Princess Linda says, "I'm going to visits the refugees in Loznica." I'm sure she did that. She told me she did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, I'm delighted we got back on the right track after that interruption a short while ago, and you and I do have the difficulty of interpretations and pauses and so on so I apologise if I seem to be interrupting you abruptly. But did you tell any of the Bosnian Serb leadership what you had seen and found in Foca or Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I fled to Pale, of course I told them. I can't remember that it was a report, not like a report that I wrote about Kupres and these visits that we already talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no report, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you were in Foca or in Zvornik, did you see or hear anything which led you to the conclusion that beyond the inevitable unhappy consequences of a violent civil conflict there had been unacceptable criminal activities by anybody?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's why I said earlier you can never, even if you write a report, you cannot say 100 per cent that something is just like that, something is so. But in a situation, to be able to know exactly what the situation was, two hours was simply not enough. The municipality and the people who worked there, when we were there we never heard anything like that from them. And I would also like to say that we insisted that we went to the hospitals is possible to see what could be done, what Princess Linda could do, actually, for the hospital. I cannot say that this wasn't so. Now that we are talking about this 14 years later, after so many articles in the newspapers that I have read after the entire material, 80 per cent of what I know now comes from here, what I have read here after I was indicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would just like to tell you, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Tell the Court --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you this. Everything is known today. I recently read a book. I do receive books. I ask for books. I want to know everything, even though I'm at the end of my life. The secret services of Serbia, from 1945 to 2005, I want to know the times in which I lived and the environment in which I lived. So there, everything is stated. The son of Sefer Halilovic, who was a boy of 8 or 9 during the war, he's a young man now, who wrote a book, and that book was a revelation for me. He's a child as far as I'm concerned, but he has stated many truths. His father also wrote a book, "Cunning Strategy," but this book is a real revelation. And when you compile all this information from various sources then you can have an idea. And I do have it and I'm very happy to have this in my head, but it's very hard to say now what you knew then and what you know now. I can say my head is full of all of these things, that I know about those events, and I can't say that I'm very happy about that, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, on what you saw and heard and found on those visits to Foca and Zvornik, was there any basis on which you could have told anybody, including the Bosnian Serb leadership, that there might have been war crimes, crimes against humanity, gratuitous killing or other violence towards civilians or any crimes of that nature?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believed that I would have some information about that. To this day I believe that the refugees in Loznica could provided more information, but I didn't go there, Princess Linda did. At that time, she spoke our language and she was not accompanied by an interpreter. She could speak our language, but I'm not sure if she could get all the finer points. But I can tell you one more thing. In that kind of situation, people, whether they were Muslim, Serb, or Croat, tended to be withdrawn and afraid to speak. When I saw that elderly women in Muslim homes kiss Arkan's hand, I laughed and I said, "You only kiss the hand of a Vladika," which is a Serbian Orthodox Bishop. And I realised they were kissing his hand out of fear. If you ask asked me, no matter how afraid I was I would never kiss his hand, even if it would save my life. But people are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mrs. Plavsic. Your Honour, I don't want to have to do this too often but if Your Honours who have that information much more readily available at the press of a button. I wonder if Your Honours could indicate how much time I have had, and then it might be, may I respectfully suggest, appropriate to renew the inquiry made of Mr. Tieger or follow it up. That was most helpful at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think from my latest report you are coming close to one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the second question. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can't be quite as die I definitive and helpful as I was last time Your Honour but I would say not a great deal. But there are a couple of things that need to be looked at but at this point I would estimate no more than 15 minutes and it might not be that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's helpful both from Your Honours and the Prosecution. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, in your statement, I wonder if you could go to paragraph 45, please. And you say there -- it's under the heading Grbavica, and you say that "In June or July, 1992, I was informed by people living in Grbavica, which was under Serb control at that time, that a person called Batko and an armed group around him were doing bad things to non-Serbs there. I understood this to mean they were submitting crimes against non-Serbs." First of all, Mrs. Plavsic, in -- from whom and in what way did that information come to you?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to attend a meeting with Mrs. Ogata that was scheduled to take place at 11.00 in Lukavica, and I was passing through a very busy intersection --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, tell us who Mrs. Ogata was? It's in your interview, I see. It's a new name in this case as far as I'm aware. Who was she, please?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Sadako Ogata was for the entire duration of the war and even after the war when she came once to see me in Banja Luka, was a representative of the United Nations dealing exclusively with matters related to refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And you were going to -- thank you for that Mrs. Plavsic. And then you were going to explain how you came by this information.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on my way to Lukavica, as I said, but time was not pressing. I started early. But this busy intersection that I mentioned is sheltered from Sarajevo by a small hill so that people met there in peace, talked, waited to see if anybody would give them a lift. And when somebody saw me in the car, a group of people started waving to me, people I didn't know. I told the driver to stop, and they told me, "Mrs. Plavsic, do you know what's going on in Grbavica?" I used to live in Grbavica, and I had fled from there. I'm not trying to say that I would not be interested in hearing about other neighbourhoods as well, but Grbavica is the closest to me because I used to live there. My university department was just across the bridge, and most of the faculty had apartments on the other side of the bridge, including myself. And I was astonished when they mentioned it. They didn't give me any details, but they said ugly things are happening in Grbavica. All the people by the way in that group who were telling me this were Serbs. And they mentioned this name, Batko. I took that very seriously indeed. I told the driver, "Let's go across the hill down there. I think we'll make it by 11.00, and then we'll go." I thought this -- this matter was going to be a priority for me, but I thought that I could do it all, including the meeting, which was very important. So I went straight to the municipality building, which was the norm the thing to do if you come to a place you don't know. Sometimes when I went to Grbavica I would go to my colleague Krunoslav Ljolja and talk to him or some of the other people. I knew many people in Grbavica. But at the municipality, they had responsibility. It was their obligation. I didn't know any of them from my past in Grbavica, so I went to see the president of municipality and told him straight away, "I was told by some Serbs here that such-and-such things are happening. Who is Batko?" That's the question I asked. They sort of looked down, wouldn't look me in the eyes. Their demeanour in itself made me suspicious. I told them that they had the responsibility, that they should take care, but I had to go. So I told them good-bye and went to see a young man whom I knew through his mother, who lived in the same building as I. The boy doesn't really know me. I was just a familiar fast. And I asked him, "Zoran, can you tell me is there a person named Batko in Grbavica?" I'm sorry for this young man. He died later. He told me, "I know. I know." And at that moment, a group came into the room led by a very stocky, short man built like a boxer, wearing a Serbian peasant hat. He was not really wearing a uniform, but he had some weapons. And he just stood there looking at me. And I decided immediately that the people from the municipality to whom I had talked must have informed him. His way of looking at me was not pleasant. Zoran took me out of the room and he said, "Mrs. Plavsic, that is Batko." After that, I left, and it never crossed my mind that anybody in Pale had any idea that there existed such a man who was threatening the lives of people in Grbavica. It was almost 11.00 by that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was his other name, this Batko?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. To this day I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your -- I don't think you need be troubled with having the piece of paper, Mrs. Plavsic, but in your interview with Mr. Nilsson, and it's tape 7, page 18, you -- there's a passage that begins -- you refer to the minister of transport in Japan, and you say, "He immediately resigned because this one railway you know, I don't know three minute was late." I'm just reading verbatim the English. "And he resigned."

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the train was three minutes late.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They do these things properly in Japan. "And when they started to defend themselves, I said no, I am not. I am the person to search for that, but you coward, you are responsible, and you need to resign immediately and to put this person in gaol." Mr. Nilsson said, "You said they were defending themselves. What did they say exactly?" And then the transcript then says, you speaking, "Ma," you see --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think -- or maybe it was me when I spoke, but I think you just skipped something. I will, if you let me, come to this Japanese train very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Japanese train is not at the core of our --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's that the train, it's is a wonderful practice, the could introduce it in the United Kingdom, but the train and the ministers resignation for it being three minutes late is not the issue, Mrs. Plavsic. I don't think I have missed anything from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, perhaps Mr. Stewart continues quoting from what is the transcript of the audio recording of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, and probably Your Honours are following it so I -- right. Thank you. Yeah, bear with me, Mrs. Plavsic, we can pick up any points, no doubt, later. It just says, for whatever reason, it says "Ma," you see, "I thought I ought to describe that Batko on that start," question mark, something on the transcript, "so, and this minister for transport, he started to laugh, 'Uh-hu, Batko.' I was shocked that they know this person. Batko was unknown for me before. First time I -- I -- I was informed that this person exists and that this person doing bad things, that altogether in one hour, and I started to describe them how this Batko looks like this minister said, 'Oh, this Batko. You know how to -- how to explain.' The only conclusion was that he's known them for long time." Mrs. Plavsic, it may seem rather silly, but are we to understand from that -- no, let me ask the question, please, are we to understand from that that Batko was personally known previously to the minister of transport for Japan?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, just let me explain. The minister of Japan -- from Japan has nothing to do with all that, nor does our minister of transport in Republika Srpska if we had one. There were two ministers involved, one Minister of Justice and the other the minister of interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic -- may I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm going to intervene at this point. In this transcript it -- it looks a bit -- at least there seems -- or there may have been some confusion. When you said, "He started to laugh. Uh-huh, Batko. I was shocked that they know this person."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Batko was unknown to me before."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Simple question: Who started to laugh and said, 'Ha, Batko'?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Minister of Justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And on what occasion exactly? Did you have a meeting at that moment with the Minister of Justice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to that meeting with Mrs. Ogata - I'm going to explain this very quickly - and all the time I was thinking that I was going to return quickly to Pale to make that meeting as short as possible, because I needed to go to Pale to inform Karadzic and Krajisnik about this, and I was thinking that everything was going according to plan, that everything was fine, because when I opened my room I opened the door of the room, I saw Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and two ministers whom I believed to be relevant to the conversation that I wanted to initiate and the report that I wanted to make. Everybody was there together. And I think I even said it in so many words, "It's good that you're all here."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who was there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Minister of Justice Mandic, Momcilo Mandic; and the minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I continue here. You then describe at least in the transcript, "I was shocked that they know this person." Who are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Minister of Justice. When I said, "Do you know, are you aware of what's going on in Grbavica? Because you should know. You'd have to know. Some person called Batko," and then the Minister of Justice smiled and said, "Oh, Batko." And after that I said, "Don't tell me that you know him." And I needed to say no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The line reads in plural, "I was shocked that they know this person." You now explained to us that you heard from the Minister of Justice that he knew who Batko was. Nevertheless, you used the plural.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both of them were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did this person know who Batko was or expressed who Batko was or was this a mistake and it was just the Minister of Justice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand your point. It was my impression that the Minister of Justice definitely knew him, because he himself said, "Uh-huh, Batko." But I also had the impression that the other minister knew him, too, the minister of the interior. I had the impression -- I mean, I thought I would be telling them something new, and instead I was telling it to some -- to people who already knew about this. So I said, "So you know about this." And then came the other point when I mentioned that Japanese train. Regardless of what's the reason, such things happen, but you are the Minister of Justice. You have to resign immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That point is taken. So you had a meeting with Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Stanisic, and Mr. Mandic. From the words spoken by Mr. Mandic, you understood that he knew who Batko was, and from the absence of any further inquiries by the others, you concluded that they were not unfamiliar with that situation regarding Batko. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, the minister of the interior at Pale should know what's going on in all of his territory let alone Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. I wouldn't say I disagree with you, but I'm just about to establish whether I correctly understood you that in this meeting by the words spoken by Mr. Mandic you observed that he knew who Batko was. And then for the others present it was on the basis of their behaviour that they concluded that they were at least aware of the situation as you describe it at that moment. If that's correctly understood, then Mr. Stewart will continue putting questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, can we just get very clear --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's me just say this: As far as Mr. Mandic is concerned, from his reaction, such as it was when he said, "Ah, Batko," I realised they all knew. Why did I mention that train? I was talking to the minister of the interior, and I said if you know this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I intervened at the time where it was time for Mr. Stewart to put questions to you. I've put one or two questions to you. I've received the answers. It's now for Mr. Stewart to focus your attention on what he'd like you to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Stewart, I am looking at the clock. If you'd say I'll try to finish in, well, I don't know - of course it's your time - within somewhere in the next 10 to 12 minutes we would continue otherwise we'll have a break now and resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I -- perhaps I might ask again for guidance as to -- because obviously the instructions of the Trial Chamber, the timing lead to -- the need for some fairly business-like calculations. First of all, may I ask Your Honour with respect, we have today, now do we, until quarter to 2.00, and quarter to 2.00 and that's it, or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we are scheduled today for the morning session, and even if it with take five or ten minutes more, that's not a matter but now try to finish this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, and so, Your Honour, that means, well, if we had five to ten minutes more that would take us to 2.00. If we had a break now, does Your Honour have in mind the usual break. We have to see Mr. Krajisnik in this break as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have the break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So we would have 70 minutes, Your Honour. Your Honour, such matters as the last few minutes -- after all, this is a clear error on the transcript of the interview, with the minister of transport for Japan being incorrectly substituted for one of the Bosnian Serb ministers. That's not really my time, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's a mistake or not but at least it gives information which is -- needs interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, if it's not a mistake, Your Honour, then we have to unravel the last ten minutes' answers. That's the only possible explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not a mistake whether they've written down but whether Mrs. Plavsic had that at times --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Understand, Your Honour, yes, I accept that entirely; a mistake on one level or another, yes, absolutely. Your Honour, it's only a little while since I asked but these are quite fine-tuned calculations. Now, how long have I had, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course I -- one second. You're approximately -- you're coming close to two hours at this moment, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We won't quibble, Your Honour, but reserve the right to quibble, if we may. Our calculation comes out slightly differently. That would leave me with 40 minutes. Your Honour, may I say this, the Prosecution then, assuming that there's not anything -- vast increase on what they indicated a short time ago, about 15 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger is nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes that's most helpful, Your Honour. Your Honour, if I said that I would therefore continue for 20 minutes after the break, would that be helpful, Your Honour, on the understanding that I then do have in reserve four the Defence time and there is then sufficient time allowed when the Prosecution have had their second bite at the cherry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest the following. We'll have a break now. We'll then resume at five minutes to 1.00. Then if you would take until a quarter past 1.00 after the break then Mr. Tieger would use approximately his 15 minutes. He's -- he had in mind and then the remaining time some additional questions can be put to you by you Mr. Stewart. The Chamber in further allotting the time and in further evaluating on how time was allotted and how -- we'll allow you to use the time always and that's, I would say, standard procedure takes into consideration also how time was used and the parties can expect the Chamber to stop no later than 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I just remind Your Honour I reserve my position in relation to that last comment as well but Your Honour I hope Your Honours haven't forgotten that the matter which I have to explore in the break now with Mr. Krajisnik is the question of questions from Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that, that that's one of the issues. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes and during the break I'll look to see if whether I need any or all of that time and we'll inform the court accordingly and just want to note that I presume that any time in -- held in reserve by Mr. Stewart is for the same purposes of the time held in reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not entirely, Your Honour. I've specifically given up some of my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I ask something? Do you have five minutes' time for me for a topic which is very far removed from all of this here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that after the break at the end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It has nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a brief remark before we continue. Time management is not one of my strongest points. It certainly is not just out of nothing, even if I may give the impression now and then. We have taken into consideration the time allotted by the parties, the time used by the parties, the balance between the parties that was on the mind of the Judges, that was one Prosecution, two for the Defence, the relevance the issues raised and the room given to the witness to expound on less relevant issues, we've taken everything into account. We proceed on the basis that, Mr. Stewart, you have your 20 minutes as asked. Then, Mr. Tieger, you'll have 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then remaining time will be not just -- just for the Defence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sure it's helpful for everyone for me to note at this time that based on the questions asked at this point I will not need any additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then since the witness also asked to add something to her statement, and it may well be that we have one or two quick questions as well, but, does this -- Mr. Stewart, in view of the fact that unless that would change on the basis of the following questions, you can then take the next 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's very kind, Your Honour. Can I just be clear? In effect the Court has -- in light of all the circumstances the Court has purported to cut my allowance and there is now 30 minutes left? Is that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, no. The remainder of the time, I had in mind the time you would have and after 30 minutes we'll have a look at whether Mr. Tieger needs any additional time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before it's not just a matter of mathematics. For example, one of the problems is how to attribute time to procedural incidents. It would go too far to give a full detail here, someone intervened for one minute, my two questions there be accounted, too; that's what I said, no arithmetics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we wanted to get started forthwith I just wanted to mention again the signing yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just would like to say, Your Honour, that the Defence reserves its position on the basis that our position is that however it's calculated and whatever consideration, taking account -- and however the arithmetic is done, we have been we have been unfairly deprived of the allocation that the court had in mind yesterday for no proper reason. But, Your Honour, obviously I now comply with Your Honour's direction and keep within that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The remainder of the time will be used as the Court deems fit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, of course. Well, it always is, ultimately, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, this -- the matter concerning Batko and Grbavica, do you know whether following your meeting back in Pale which you say Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and the two ministers, Stanisic and Mandic, were present, do you know whether any action was in fact taken officially against Batko?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So would it come as a surprise to you to know that indeed it was and that after proposals made by military security ultimately Batko's activities were stopped by official organs? Would that surprise you to know that?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't finish. So let me say it now. I did have a way of finding out whether he was still active there, and I received information. How I obtained the information is not important now. Batko stopped his activities. Batko is still at Grbavica, and then for a month I received this information, and then a man told me Batko has disappeared from Grbavica. How? I have just heard from you, as you say, if it's the military police or something like that. What I was interested in is whether he was still doing what he was doing. But he stopped then. He probably got scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a dangerous man.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And from that time on my life was in danger but -- and it wasn't just from him, by Mandic as well. He -- actually, there were open threats against me and my brother. There were threats that my brother would be killed because in that way I would suffer more than if we were to kill me. I'm glad to hear you say that it was the military police. I didn't know that. All I knew was that it had stopped, and I believed the person whom I entrusted with monitoring what was going on at Grbavica, because I as a member of the Presidency did not have access to information, official information. Ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... visit to Grbavica to look into this Batko issue been an official visit or had you just gone on your own initiative without reference to any other official organs?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the Presidency. They knew that, the people in Grbavica, and it was generally known. I said earlier that many of my colleagues from university had apartments at Grbavica. I had a schoolmate from elementary school. He was a Muslim, at the university, and when we, let's say even got old he was there with his wife. And of course I am answering the question. I'm answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic. Mr. Stewart, did I miss something? I heard the testimony to be that Mrs. Plavsic was on her way to a meeting at Lukavica, that at a crossroad or she was stopped by people informing her that there was a Batko doing bad things, that she then instructed her driver to go over the hill and to see what happened on the other side. Have I misunderstood it? Because ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, that's helpful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore what.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour's point is correct I'll move on if I may then to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is what I mean, relevance and efficiency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right about that one. Well done, Your Honour. You are right. That's helpful. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. -- Mrs. Plavsic, the -- you had -- in your interview you had said -- you said to Mr. Karadzic, and this is page 19, tape 7, "Batko in gaol or these two ministers," by which you meant Mandic and Stanisic. From your point of view at that time, if Batko's activities were definitely stopped, then that would have been all concerned performing their primary duty to make sure these things didn't happen, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the ministers were not performing their duties because Batko should have been arrested and brought to trial. When I heard that his activities had stopped but when I heard that he was still at Grbavica after that, I couldn't understand that. There was no need for any special laws of war. You know, in the state of war, all laws are much stricter, but regular laws had to be respected. If someone was harassing people, killing people, it don't mean that once he stopped doing that he was free to walk around. His presence was something that frightened people. I'm not a person that's easily scared, but I'll tell you, I was scared. Can you imagine how others felt?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What -- in what way was your life indicated to you to be in danger in some way at the hands of -- or instigation of Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic sent me a message to be very careful when starting the engine of the car. You know very well. I mean he probably meant explosives. Later, openly, he was so powerful and he was so unafraid and it was so terrible that he said, "I changed my plan. I'm not going to kill her. I'm going to kill her brother instead, because that way she would suffer more."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where did he say that and to whom?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my driver. I didn't have an escort or anything like that. I believed that that was not necessary, but I did have a loyal driver, and he was afraid. After that, I told him, "You have children. I have to tell you, even though I'm a member of the Presidency and even though you are doing this job officially and you're driving me, you have to decide. I really cannot vouch for your life." And he did stay with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, I -- I -- I hope and take it that in fact no harm did come to your brother. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, thank God. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I hand to you, please, your -- your book, the one that is referred to in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's actually Mr. Krajisnik's copy. I hope Mrs. Plavsic is happy to use that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While it's handed out I can inform the parties that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have a copy. Just tell me the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. [Previous translation continues] ... his own copy. Then thank you very much, Mrs. Plavsic. He can have that back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While this is being done, I inform the parties that the comparison between the two statements did not show any further differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And we appreciate that being done so quickly, Your Honour. That's most helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, could you turn, please, to page 286.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of the book, yes. And this is one of the passages which has been referred to in your statement and translated. And I'd like you to fine the paragraph that begins in English "Twelve years later at the Krajisnik trial in The Hague." Do you see that reference?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. I know. I know it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Twelve years later --" you wrote it, Mrs. Plavsic, "Twelve years later at the Krajisnik trial in The Hague a transcript of his conversation with Mladic from 1992 was read. It revealed that military equipment was being actively smuggled to the Muslims at the time. He suspected some army members and said, 'If this is true as I have heard, then there's no hope for the Serbian people.'" First of all, Mrs. Plavsic, just to be clear, are you able to follow the course of this trial in the prison in Sweden?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I receive newspapers from Belgrade, state newspapers, central newspaper, the newspaper political as well as Glas Javnosti and Vecernje Novosti. These are three daily newspapers. From Banja Luka I receive --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, the -- there is implicit injunction from the Trial Chamber that I should try to keep your answers short and -- to my questions. So your source of information about the Krajisnik trial is -- is just what you read in newspapers described to you, is that -- the answer to that question is yes, is it?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. And then we continue, "I fully agree with what Krajisnik said then, that there was no hope for our people because of that but neither for any other people who trade with the enemy during a war. Not because the enemy will be stronger but because this means total moral erosion of individuals, the leadership, and the society. Why did Momo not say so and support me when I spoke about it at the Assembly? Because he was also involved in all this together with Karadzic. And why did he warn Mladic in 1992 that some military personnel were also involved? Because in this way he shifted the suspicion from the civilian authorities to the military leadership. The president of the republic said openly in front of the deputies that this had to be. On several occasions, I heard our soldiers on the front line near Momo's house say that they were not going to be able to resist for much longer the temptation to shell his house which the Muslims were protecting as if it were theirs. They also said that the house was full of ammunition and weapons for sale. They asked me to tell Krajisnik that they would blow his house up. I think they did at end the of the war. I did not pass on the soldiers' messages but invited them to come to a meeting of the Assembly and tell the deputies what they had told me. I said this at an Assembly and those involved in the sale gave them an affirmative answer." First of all, Mrs. Plavsic, when you were told by these soldiers about what was apparently a considerable arms cache at Mr. Krajisnik's house, did you believe them?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That wasn't my question --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, Mrs. Plavsic. I have very limited time now, please, my question was did you believe them?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But I told them to come to the Assembly and say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you have any doubts, although you believed them as you did, did you nevertheless have any doubts as to whether what they were telling you might or might not be true?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you reject immediately in your own mind any question of taking it up with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I clarified that at a much higher level. Before 80 deputies it I put that question: Is it possible that ammunition and weapons are being sold to our enemy? And the answer from President Karadzic was -- he was very irritated by that, and I know that it was a very direct and courageous question at that time, but I wanted to hear that from an official, and he said, "Yes." I said, "Must that be so if we're selling food which is coming as part of the humanitarian aid? Must we also sell weapons?" I was stimulated to do that, because a woman who was working at the factory, working on a specific profile of weapon, a specific bullet, came to me and she said, "This bullet that I made, because it carries a particular number, and my brother was killed in the past two days, and perhaps I myself manufactured the bullet that killed my brother." That was not the only such case either. I announced that to the assembly, and the answer I got was yes. And I said if food had to be sold, must ammunition be sold as well? The answer was, "Yes, it must." What could I do?.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't ask me that any more. It's an enormous tragedy, and I poured all of that into this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm afraid I reserve the right to ask you anything relevant, Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And excuse me, but when I read in the newspaper -- in the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... restrain Mrs. Plavsic because I have so little time left, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, Mrs. Plavsic, at the end of your testimony you will have an opportunity to -- as you asked, for five minutes to add what you'd like to raise, but at this time Mr. Stewart is entitled to ask you questions. Would you please focus on answering his questions. Please proceed Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, you -- this is clear from your interviews: You did and have felt excluded and had since early on in the war felt excluded by your Bosnian Serb colleagues at times because you were a woman, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never suffered from that. We lived in a traditional environment where such an approach is that -- actually, there are some conversations that you do not conduct in front of women, so how can you have a woman in politics now, and how -- but I think that that wasn't the problem, because at the multi-party elections I received the highest number of votes from -- out of all the Serbian candidates, which does not reflect this traditional view. But the war had come and there is a lot of that and since I'm part of that environment I do have an understanding of it and perhaps that's what they also thought in the leadership. We are just going to give her some humanitarian work, and we are going to be doing men's work. And to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm struggling to keep Mrs. Plavsic to my questions in the remaining time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Turn to page 113, 1-1-3, of your own book, please. See a paragraph beginning "Koljevic and I"?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Koljevic and I were asked to establish contact." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Koljevic -- I'd like a short answer to this, please, Mrs. Plavsic, in the first place. Koljevic was somebody in whom you had considerable confidence and trust, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't talk about trust, but we've had similar views.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's enough for my purposes, Mrs. Plavsic. The -- immediate purposes. Six or seven lines do you -- you say, "The duties I was entrusted with by the Assembly were entirely taken over by Krajisnik." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Most likely an agreement with Radovan and some other party officials. They all believed, and these are traditional ideas, that there was no place for a woman in these times just before the war, and especially not in wartime." That was a fair summary of how you felt was it?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the time that this information from the soldiers about the arms cache came up how late in 1992 was that? You say it's late 1992. It's not absolutely clear from the text. Do you remember when abouts it was? All right it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- matter. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not in 1992, for sure. This was later, information about trading in ammunition. I think that was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you think this information about the cache of arms in Mr. Krajisnik's house that was later you say? Later than 1992? Correct? Are you --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me say this: I had to hear that at least from five sides, not just that, but many other things for me to then accept it. Then I went to the Assembly and asked if this was true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So 1992 probably passed as the time when I was thinking about these things. I just simply couldn't believe that. I kept saying, "that's impossible, that's impossible." But later it turned out it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mrs. Plavsic, I make it clear Mr. Krajisnik's position is it was impossible because there was no such cache of ammunition and weapons in his house. That's what I put to you. But first of all Mrs. Plavsic you have no idea, have you, whether that is or isn't true yourself.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The front line was there. That was some kind of border. I wasn't at that border.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you fighters were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You have no idea yourself whether or not that was true, have you?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is true. If somebody cheats you once, twice, the third time and keeps saying the same thing over and over again and then the fourth time then -- sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question that is put to you at this moment is that you said, "I believed what they told me." Is there, apart from your feeling, having been cheated or not? I mean, do you have any objective information which would support what those said at that time to you? So supporting beyond just believing what you were told.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to put it briefly, it's not my personal knowledge. The same way that you asked me yesterday or the day before whether they within to see Milosevic. I didn't follow them. I wasn't in the room. So it's not based on personal knowledge. But I told you in what way I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So here I think we're talking about same category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you consider any alternative way of dealing with this matter based on what you were told soldiers to go to the Assembly and publicly open up this issue without even approaching Mr. Krajisnik, without taking any steps to see whether this extreme allegation against one of your colleagues in the leadership had any truth at all? Did you consider such an alternative?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To this day I believe that I told it to them best, in the best possible way. The Assembly is a public place, so they could have done it the way I did it before the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' request. We hear a lot of shuffling of papers in the headphones it drowns out the witness's voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's me. I'm just about to stop shuffling altogether for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you go to page 85 of your book, please, Mrs. Plavsic. You've just talked about -- you've just talked about a rift between Banja Luka SDS and SDS central office, and then there's a paragraph beginning, do you see "There were people particularly -- particularly in the Krajina"? Do you see a paragraph beginning -- do you see that? Do you see that will paragraph? Yes.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think it's going on page 85.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, did I say -- I thought I said 85. Well, as a matter of fact, I did. It's page 85. You have the paragraph, do you?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 85. Yes, Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's not on 85? Well, according to the translation, really --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was only trying to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think it goes over the page no I appreciate help is being given a I think the paragraph starts at 85 it probably goes over to 86. Yes. There's a paragraph beginning "There were people particularly in the Krajina." Do a you see that? "Who knew about his criminal record and who later learned a about Krajisnik's criminal record as well. I became aware of those periods in their lives when war was already in full swing and after I fled Sarajevo for Pale towards the end of May, 1992, I had been offered a to read the records but I refused to admit that something like that could a possibly exist." What criminal record did Mr. Krajisnik have, Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the time you're talking about in your book, you say you've heard a about this, what criminal record did Mr. Krajisnik have?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in 1992. Before I knew that somebody with the name of a Krajisnik and somebody with the name of Karadzic are living there in Sarajevo. It was a time when I was involved in completely different work that was going on, and it was reported in newspapers, I think. However, when I went to Pale --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, let's look at what you've written. "There were people, particularly" the previous paragraph you're talking?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The previous paragraph you're talking all about the rift between Banja Luka and Sarajevo, I am -- and you say "(I am speaking of 1991.)" That's what it says. The very next one you say, "there were people particularly in the Krajina who knew about his criminal record," that's somebody else, "and you later learned about Krajisnik's criminal record as well." We can bring it up-to-date, Mrs. Plavsic. Mr. Krajisnik is on trial here what criminal record do you say Mr. Krajisnik has ever had?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ask him. He knows much better than I.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't need to ask him Ms. Plavsic. Mr. Krajisnik has no criminal record and I therefore ask you to accept -- see if you do accept now, that it is grossly irresponsible to have you -- let me finish. I'm asking you to accept, please, it is grossly irresponsible for you, especially for a man that Mr. Krajisnik is in, which he was when you wrote this book, to go putting such false information in your book. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not false at all. It's not false at all. There is a record, and I think it was maybe 1987, and that was the time when the two of them became close. They were in remand, in a remand prison for -- for some months, and I learned about that when I fled to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Krajisnik -- I'm so sorry. Mrs. Plavsic, do you know that they were acquitted and do you know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. -- Mr. Stewart, I'm going to stop you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you know that it happened. I thought you were simply uninformed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you can put this to the witness and then you should quote the full paragraph. The full paragraph, and I'll read it to you, what you -- perhaps you'll read it with me. "There were people, particularly in the Krajina, who knew about his criminal record and who later learned about Krajisnik's criminal record as well. I became aware of those periods in their lives when war was already in full swing and after I fled Sarajevo for Pale towards the end of May, 1992. I had been offered to read the records but I refused to admit that something like that could possibly exist. And if it did, I felt it would hurt and disorient me. I can only imagine how ordinary people would take it. Anyway, it now seems irrelevant compared to the terrible tragedy that has befallen us." Where there are suggestions in your question, Mr. Stewart, that the book here states as a fact that Mrs. Plavsic accepts a criminal record, which is by the way a term which is multi-interpretable as well, then that would be something the Chamber would have difficulties to accept without any reservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First Your Honour I did read at lines 15 to 16, I read, "As far as I refuse to admit something like that could possibly exist." So the nub of the point Your Honour has just been making in my submission I did fairly include in my citation from that paragraph. In the interests of time, I did not go on to the rest of the paragraph which I did not consider significantly affected the point. Maybe Your Honour was right about that, maybe I was wrong. But that was and is still my position. So far as Your Honour's interpretation of the text, I'm not going to argue that in front of the witness, Your Honour; no doubt at some other time. But I may observe that the witness has not resiled from the assertion that Mr. Krajisnik had a criminal record one bit but has in fact persisted with that contention in this court. And I'm so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I'm out of time and I've finished, Your Honour. It becomes matter of argument now. I've asked Mrs. Plavsic those questions but maybe I'm to be given instructions by my client.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nevertheless, I have to tell you, please, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not being given specific instructions in relation to my cross-examination, Your Honour. Your Honour knows our position. We never in fact resiled from the position that cross-examination ought to be limited to cross-examination by counsel, but we live with the rulings that have been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any -- you have not been instructed. Then there was an issue that you would discuss with Mr. Krajisnik whether there would be any questions he would like to put and that should be questions which would not have been foreseen and which could not have been discussed in the normal way with counsel. I'm just verifying at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I verify two or three things, Your Honour. I understand although Mr. Josse and I thought differently a moment ago, I understand I'm not being offered specific instructions by Mr. Krajisnik. Now as to questions I as his counsel should put, which is the normal course, I have also Your Honour of course in the break and when I've had previous opportunities to discuss with Mr. Krajisnik the whole issues of questions to Mrs. Plavsic, I'm bound to say Your Honour that the idea that in the time available and in the circumstances we could have come anywhere near almost doing more than just starting that exercise just impossible as it happens so we are left with -- we were left at the end of the break with unresolved issues as far as that goes so Your Honour the position is I believe that Mr. Krajisnik himself which is where we are because counsel would rather step aside in accordance with Your Honour's rulings here. But Mr. Krajisnik himself has something to say on this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik. Is there any -- my question to you first would be is there any question you'd like to put to the witness which could not reasonably have been put through counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you are on notice of what I said yesterday please keep that in mind. Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Krajisnik might put a few questions to you as well. I instruct you that -- not to enter into any debate. Listen to the question. Try to answer the question as factual as possible, and if you feel that you have difficulties in doing so, please address me and do not enter into a debate with Mr. Krajisnik, because this is, as I said before, is not a debating club. Mr. Krajisnik. Cross-examination by the Accused Krajisnik:

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good day, Biljana.

utterances.speaker: BILJANA PLAVSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will not speak about the book. I'm one of those who read -- excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, no introductory comments whether you'll speak about the book or not. Put questions. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I haven't seen Mrs. Biljana for such a long time. I can't keep down to two or three sentences, and otherwise I'll abide by your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may put questions to Mrs. Plavsic. Nothing else. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right I will not ask questions about the book just some questions I believe are a matter of misunderstanding. You said yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this is the last warning. I will deprive you from the right to put any questions to the witness if you are telling her to start with whether it's an about misunderstandings, about books, or not. Put questions to Mrs. Plavsic if you want to use that right. We allow you that right. And a strict ruling that should abide by rules and that is put a question and do not give comments before you start putting a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to protest, Your Honour. If you don't let me ask the question then say so. I will ask my question very properly and abide by your rules but please allow me to finish my sentence. If I can't do that then I can't ask the question. I don't want any sort of confrontation.
